title: Ποιμὴν καὶ λυκιδεῖς
part: The Shepherd and the Wolf-Cubs (Chambry 313 · Perry 209)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 313 (= Perry 209). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποιμὴν εὑρὼν λυκιδεῖς, τούτους μετὰ πολλῆς ἐπιμελείας ἔτρεφεν, οἰόμενος ὅτι τελειωθέντες οὐ μόνον τὰ ἑαυτοῦ πρόβατα τηρήσουσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἕτερα ἀρπάζοντες αὐτῷ οἴσουσιν.
sentences.tr: Poimēn heurōn lykideis, toutous meta pollēs epimeleias etrephen, oiomenos hoti teleiōthentes ou monon ta heautou probata tērēsousin, alla kai hetera arpazontes autōi oisousin.
sentences.l: A shepherd, having found wolf-cubs, reared them with much care, thinking that, once brought to full growth, they would not only keep his own sheep safe, but would also, snatching others, bring them to him.
sentences.i: A shepherd found some wolf-cubs and reared them with great care, thinking that when they were fully grown they would not only guard his own sheep but would snatch other sheep as well and bring them to him.
sentences.n: οἴομαι takes ὅτι with a finite verb here, where the infinitive would be the older construction. τελειωθέντες is the aorist passive participle of τελειόω, 'be brought to completion', used of animals reaching full growth. The futures τηρήσουσιν and οἴσουσιν keep the tense the shepherd's own thought had. Chambry prints ἀρπάζοντες with a smooth breathing, where ἁρπάζω regularly takes a rough one; the printed form is kept.

sentences.t: Οἱ δέ, ὡς τάχιστα ηὐξήθησαν, ἀδείας τυχόντες πρῶτον αὐτοῦ τὴν ποίμνην διαφθείρειν ἤρξαντο.
sentences.tr: Hoi de, hōs tachista ēuxēthēsan, adeias tychontes prōton autou tēn poimnēn diaphtheirein ērxanto.
sentences.l: But they, as soon as ever they had grown, having met with a free hand, began to destroy his flock first of all.
sentences.i: But as soon as they were grown, and had nothing to fear, the first flock they set about destroying was his.
sentences.n: ὡς τάχιστα with the aorist is 'as soon as ever'. τυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one lights upon, and ἄδεια is freedom from fear of punishment, a free hand. πρῶτον belongs with what follows: his flock is the first they ruin, not the last.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὡς ταῦτα ᾔσθετο, ἀναστενάξας εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε δίκαια πέπονθα· τί γὰρ τούτους νηπίους ὄντας ἔσῳζον οὓς ἔδει καὶ ηὐξημένους ἀναιρεῖν ; »
sentences.tr: Kai hōs tauta ēistheto, anastenaxas eipen· « All’ egōge dikaia pepontha· ti gar toutous nēpious ontas esōizon hous edei kai ēuxēmenous anairein ; »
sentences.l: And when he perceived this, groaning aloud he said: « But I for my part have suffered what is just: why did I go on saving these while they were helpless young, whom one had to destroy even when full-grown? »
sentences.i: And when he saw it, he groaned aloud and said: « But I have got no more than my deserts. Why did I keep these creatures alive while they were helpless young, when even full-grown they ought to have been killed? »
sentences.n: δίκαια πέπονθα uses the neuter plural adjective as an internal accusative, 'I have suffered what is just'. ἔδει, imperfect of δεῖ, is the regular Greek for what ought to have been done and was not. καὶ ηὐξημένους is 'even when they had grown': if the grown wolf must be killed, all the more the cub.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ τοὺς πονηροὺς περισῴζοντες λανθάνουσι καθ’ ἑαυτῶν πρῶτον αὐτοὺς ῥωννύντες.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi tous ponērous perisōizontes lanthanousi kath’ heautōn prōton autous rhōnnyntes.
sentences.l: So those who bring the wicked safely through escape their own notice making them strong first of all against themselves.
sentences.i: So those who preserve the wicked make them strong against themselves before anyone else, and never notice they are doing it.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle is the Greek idiom for doing a thing unawares: the participle ῥωννύντες carries the action and the verb says only that it went unseen. The same turn closes fables 87 and 270. καθ’ ἑαυτῶν, 'down against themselves', is the hostile κατά with the genitive.
